item.title: 01 Sensation & Perception
item.description: Definition: When a stimulus activates the receptors of a sense organ; awareness of changing conditions.Something that causes a bodily response Definition: Weakest amount of a stimulus required to produce a sensation Key fact: Detected 50% of the time Definition: Minimum amount of difference a person can detect between two stimuli Example: Optometrist testing your vision The larger/stronger a stimulus, the greater the change needed to notice any difference.Definition: Get used to the level of a sensation and respond only to changes away from it Survival Prevent overstimulation Example: Vision adapts in darker areas Definition: Tendency to detect the presence of stimuli correctly due to motivation, skill, and competing stimuli Key argument: Argues against a single threshold Pre-attentive (automatic): Unconscious processing Attentive (careful attention): Conscious, deliberate focus Definition: The way we interpret sensations and organize them into meaningful experiences.Examples: Seeing a car Hearing a song on the radio Feeling a desk Perception is shaped by more than the raw sensory input we receive. It is influenced by: Needs: When we want something, we are more likely to perceive it Beliefs and expectations: We tend to notice things that fit what we already believe Previous experience: Past experience helps us interpret new sensory information These factors help construct the brain's perception tools, which allow us to make sense of the world quickly and efficiently.The brain automatically tries to organize separate pieces of information into wholes.Five Gestalt Principles: Proximity: Things that are close together are seen as belonging together Continuity: The brain prefers smooth, continuous patterns Similarity: Similar things are grouped together Simplicity: The brain favors the simplest interpretation possible Closure: The brain fills in missing information to complete a whole The ability to distinguish between a figure and its background.Examples in senses other than sight: Walking into a bakery and smelling cinnamon while filtering out every other smell Eating a big meal and being able to taste the lemon inside of it Retinal disparity: The difference between the images each eye receives; a binocular cue that helps the brain compute depth (greater disparity = closer object). Convergence: Eyes turn inward (converge) for near objects; feedback from the eye muscles provides a cue to depth and distance. Constancy: Perceive objects as stable and unchanging despite changes in viewing angle, distance, or lighting. Common forms include size constancy, shape constancy, and brightness (color) constancy. Illusions: Perceptions that incorrectly represent physical stimuli; visual illusions reveal how perceptual systems use cues and assumptions, sometimes producing systematic errors. Notes: The attached slide images illustrate retinal disparity (different images from each eye) and shape/size constancy examples (doors shown from different angles). These visual examples highlight how multiple cues and automatic perceptual rules interact to create our stable sense of the environment.

item.title: Temporal Lobe
item.description: Location: Sides of brain, near temples (left and right) Location: Superior temporal lobe Function: Processes sound frequencies Processes: Pitch, volume, tone, speech sounds Location: Left temporal lobe (superior temporal gyrus)Function: Understanding spoken and written language Hippocampus: Long-term memory formation Amygdala: Emotional memory Stores: Autobiographical memories, facts, events Receives: Auditory input from primary auditory cortex Processes: Meaning of words and sentences Connects: To Broca's area for language production Connects: To hippocampus for memory Recognizes emotional meaning of words/tones Links sounds to emotional memories Inferior temporal regions Recognizes familiar faces Damage = prosopagnosia (can't recognize faces) Right temporal lobe for melody Left temporal for rhythm Musical memory storage Most common type of focal seizure May cause: Auditory hallucinations Déjà vu Emotional changes Memory disruption Temporal lobes (hippocampus) severely affected Memory loss is primary symptom Progressive language comprehension decline

item.title: Big Five Personality Model
item.description: Most well-known trait theory; most empirically supportedFive central dimensions applicable to ALL peopleSpectrum: Open-minded ←→ Closed-mindedSpectrum: Responsible ←→ CarelessSpectrum: Outgoing ←→ ReservedSpectrum: Sympathetic ←→ CruelSpectrum: Moody ←→ Calm/RelaxedEveryone's Big Five score is different:Example Profile 1:O: High C: High E: Low A: High N: Low = Creative, organized introvert; dependable, calm (Good for: Research, writing, focused work) Example Profile 2:O: Low C: Low E: High A: High N: High = Spontaneous, talkative; anxious, cooperative (Good for: People-oriented work with support) ✓ Empirically supported: Most research of any model ✓ Cross-cultural: Works across cultures ✓ Stable: Traits remain relatively consistent ✓ Comprehensive: Captures major personality variation ✓ Practical: Used in business, clinical, research ✓ Easy to measure: Standardized questionnaires ✓ Predictive: Predicts important outcomes ✗ Doesn't explain why traits exist ✗ Ignores situational influences ✗ Self-report biases ✗ May miss cultural-specific traits ✗ Doesn't address values, motivations ✗ Assumes stability (people change) ✗ Reductionist (is personality really just these 5?) 240 items Most comprehensive Research standard 44 items Shorter, practical Widely used Various online versions Quick assessment Less precise than above Used in hiring Team building Leadership development Career counseling

item.title: Cognitive Personality Theory
item.description: Core Principle: Ideas of oneself, others, and the world shape personalitiesDefinition: Mental representation of people, events, and concepts Mental templates: Internal organization of information Patterns: Recognizable sequences or categories Organization: How we structure knowledge Predictive: Help us anticipate what comes next Person has schema: "People are judgmental" Same situation, different schemas = different personalities Schemas can be accurate or distorted Persistent schemas shape personality consistency Definition: Beliefs about yourself; the most important schema Consistency: Act in ways that match self-image Selective attention: Notice information confirming self-view Interpretation: Interpret ambiguous events as supporting self-schema Memory: Remember things consistent with self-schema Goal selection: Choose activities matching self-concept Internal: "I failed because I'm stupid" (personality-based) External: "I failed because the test was hard" (situation-based) Determines: Self-esteem and future motivation Confirmation bias: Seek info confirming existing beliefs Negativity bias: Weight negative info more Projection: Assume others think like us Same stressor, different appraisals = different personality responses "Challenge" vs. "threat" appraisal changes behavior Personality shows through how we think about situations Identify unhelpful thoughts Challenge their accuracy Replace with more accurate thoughts Result: Personality changes Before: Thought: "Everyone judges me" Behavior: Withdrawn, anxious Personality: Shy, anxious Restructuring: Challenge: "Evidence they judge me?" New thought: "Some people are friendly" New behavior: Social attempts New personality: More outgoing ✓ Testable and researched ✓ Explains personality change ✓ Clear intervention path (change thoughts → change personality) ✓ Applies to depression, anxiety, personality disorders ✗ May overestimate conscious thought influence ✗ Doesn't account for temperament/biology ✗ Assumes rationality (people not always rational) ✗ Ignores emotional and behavioral factors

item.title: Humanistic Personality Theory
item.description: Core Principle: People naturally strive for self-actualization (achieving their unique potential)Definition: Fulfilling one's unique potential; becoming the best version of oneselfHierarchy of NeedsPersonality Implications: People with unmet lower needs → anxious, focused on survival People with met basic needs → can pursue growth Self-actualization is highest human motivation Focus: "The Self" and client-centered therapyDefinition: Person's perception of their own nature, abilities, and worthDefinition: Evaluation of yourself based on how others respond to youDefinition: Specific conditions you must meet to feel valued by important peopleDefinition: Perception that significant others value you completely, without condition With unconditional regard: Authentic, confident, actualized With conditional regard: Self-conscious, anxious, inauthentic Parenting role: Provide foundation for healthy personality Realistic: See self and world accurately (not distorted) Accepting: Acknowledge limitations and imperfections Natural: Don't pretend; be authentic Creative: Solve problems in novel ways Independent: Don't need constant approval Purposeful: Work toward meaningful goals Empathetic listener Non-judgmental Provide unconditional positive regard Reflect back what they hear Help client find own answers ✓ Emphasizes potential for growth ✓ Explains motivation for achievement ✓ Supportive approach proves effective ✓ Respects individual differences ✗ Vague concepts (hard to define, measure) ✗ Overly optimistic about human nature ✗ Limited empirical research ✗ Doesn't account for mental illness biology ✗ "Self-actualization" looks different for everyone ✗ Assumes everyone can overcome obstacles with support

item.title: Language Development
item.description: Baby hears words Attempts to repeat sounds Not yet understand meaning Random trial and error Child learns rule ("add -ed for past tense") Over-applies rule: "goed", "eated" Actually a sign of learning! Example: All animals are "doggy" Child learns exceptions Uses grammar correctly Flexible, creative use of language Can understand novel sentences Definition: Sensitive period early in life when language acquisition is easier Peak: Birth to 3-5 years Still possible: Beyond critical period, but harder Bilingual advantage: Learning multiple languages easier during critical period Later learning: Possible (like second language) but different process Evidence: Children with minimal language exposure struggle later Second language accent harder to eliminate after 7-8 years Early exposure helps native-like proficiency Conversation (not just TV) most effective Back-and-forth interaction crucial Emotional connection enhances learning Learning two languages simultaneously possible May have smaller vocabulary in each, but larger total Bilingual advantages: Cognitive flexibility, metalinguistic awareness

item.title: Motor Development
item.description: Definition: Maturation — internally programmed growth of a child; plays a key role in progress of motor skillsKey Principle: Cephalocaudal (head to tail) developmentKey Principle: Proximodistal (near to far) development Determines readiness: Baby must be neurologically ready Sets sequence: Order is largely fixed Provides capability: Brain and muscles must be capable Accelerates slightly: Practice helps, but only after ready Cannot reverse order: Can't crawl before trunk control ready Refines skills: Once capable, practice improves ability Too early: Child not ready, cannot do skill Right time: Skill emerges naturally with practice After maturation: Still develops, but more effortful Space to move: Room to explore Safe environment: Freedom without danger Opportunities: Varied surfaces, objects to manipulate Encouragement: Adult support and attention Nutrition: Adequate protein and calories Sleep: Needed for neurological development Exercise: Movement strengthens muscles, builds connections Tummy time: Strengthens neck and shoulder muscles Play: Encourages practice of emerging skills Safety: Protection from obstacles while exploring Responsiveness: Motivation to move and explore Some babies walk at 10 months, others at 15 months All within normal range Usually not predictive of later abilities Genetics influence development rate Not rolling by 6 months Not sitting by 9 months Not walking by 18 months Significant asymmetry (one side lagging) Early intervention can help Brain plasticity highest in infancy Small delays can become larger gaps without support

item.title: Myers-Briggs Type Indicator
item.description: Based on Carl Jung's personality types; popular but scientifically controversialHow you interact with the worldHow you gather informationHow you make decisionsHow you organize lifeCombination of 4 dimensions = 16 typesE/I × S/N × T/F × J/P = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 combinations ✓ Widely used in career counseling ✓ Fun, engaging, self-insight ✓ Provides framework for understanding differences ✓ Good conversation starter ✓ Many online resources Easy to remember 4-letter type Validates personal differences Suggests career paths Explains relationship dynamics Non-judgmental framework ✗ Low test-retest reliability: Different results on repeat ✗ Limited predictive validity: Doesn't predict outcomes well ✗ Dichotomous thinking: Forces choices (I/E) that aren't binary ✗ Insufficient research: Far fewer studies than Big Five ✗ Overstated simplicity: People claim certain behaviors impossible for their type ✗ Misuse as excuse: "I'm an INTJ so I'm blunt" (deterministic) ✓ Good for thinking about preferences ✓ Useful in career exploration ✓ Conversation about personality ✓ Personal insight ✗ Not rigorously validated ✗ Unreliable over time ✗ Can't predict behavior well ✗ Oversimplifies personality Widely popular in business/counseling Criticized by personality psychologists Not supported as diagnostic tool Used despite scientific limitations Career exploration starting point Team awareness building General self-reflection Ice breaker activities Clinical diagnosis Personnel selection (legally risky) Serious psychological assessment Major life decisions MBTI is entertaining and can prompt self-reflection, but it's not scientifically rigorous. For serious personality assessment, the Big Five is more reliable and researched.Think of MBTI as a fun personality framework that captures something real about how people differ, but not as psychological truth the way Big Five is.

item.title: Neurons & Neurotransmitters
item.description: Function: Stores and protects DNA Produces: mRNA for protein synthesis Makes: Proteins needed for neuron function Function: Creates energy for neuron Contains: Mitochondria (powerhouses) Integrates: Signals from dendrites Structure: Fatty insulation around axon Function: Speeds up electrical impulses Protection: Protects axon from damage Benefit: Makes neural transmission 10-100x faster Location: End of axon Function: Release neurotransmitters Structure: Vesicles containing neurotransmitters Definition: Chemical messengers produced in neurons that transmit information between brain cells Too much or too little linked to disorders Medications often target neurotransmitter levels Lifestyle affects neurotransmitter production Excess linked to: Alzheimer's disease Normal role: Learning, memory, movement Problem: Buildup disrupts neural function Excess linked to: Schizophrenia Normal role: Motivation, reward, movement Problem: Excessive dopamine = hallucinations, delusions Deficiency linked to: Parkinson's disease Normal role: Motivation, movement control Problem: Loss of motor control, reduced motivation Deficiency linked to: Depression Normal role: Mood regulation, sleep, appetite Problem: Low mood, sleep disruption, anxiety Excitatory signals encourage neuron firing Inhibitory signals prevent neuron firing Both types necessary for proper function Too much excitation = seizures Too much inhibition = paralysis/coma

item.title: Occipital Lobe
item.description: Location: Very back of brain (posterior/occipital pole)Location: First visual processing area (back of occipital lobe)Function: Analyzes basic visual featuresPrinciple: Visual field maps directly onto visual cortexResult: Cortex contains distorted "map" of visual world Route: Occipital → Temporal lobe Function: Object identification Question: "What am I looking at?" Example: Recognizing a face as your friend Route: Occipital → Parietal lobe Function: Spatial location and movement Question: "Where is it / where is it going?" Example: Tracking a moving car Scotoma: Blind spot in visual field (often triangular) Loss is retinotopic: Corresponds to location of damage Rest of vision: Usually preserved Can see all basic features Cannot recognize what they're looking at "Visual object agnosia" = see but don't recognize Damage not to V1 but to connections to temporal lobe Massive bilateral occipital damage Can lead to complete blindness Some patients have "blindsight" (detect movement without awareness) Specific regions respond to specific colors V4 area specialized for color Color perception involves occipital + temporal processing Usually retinal (cone cells lack pigment) Rarely due to cortical damage alone Middle temporal area (MT/V5) processes motion Detects direction and speed Essential for tracking moving objects Akinetopsia: Motion blindness Can't see movement (see "snapshots") Extremely rare with cortical damage Dangerous (can't judge approaching cars) Occipital lobe hyperactivity Visual disturbances (zigzag lines, blind spots) Followed by headache Visual hallucinations Flashing lights, geometric patterns Often start in back of visual field

item.title: Parenting Styles
item.description: Definition: Characteristic patterns of parental attitudes and behaviors that create an emotional climate for parent-child interactionApproach: "My way or the highway" High demands Low responsiveness Little discussion Strict rules Punishment-oriented ✗ Obedient but not independent ✗ Lower self-esteem ✗ May rebel or become anxious ✗ Difficulty making decisions ✗ Limited creativity Approach: "Do whatever you want" Low demands High responsiveness Few boundaries Few rules/limits Child-centered decisions ✗ Difficulty with self-control ✗ Struggle with authority later ✗ Higher anxiety (lack structure) ✗ May be self-centered ✗ Impulsivity issues Approach: "I don't really care" Low demands Low responsiveness Neglectful Parent's needs prioritized Minimal involvement ✗ Insecure attachment ✗ Behavioral problems ✗ Low self-esteem ✗ Social difficulties ✗ Academic struggles ✗ Emotional regulation problems Approach: "I'm involved in everything" ✗ Difficulty with independence ✗ Higher anxiety ✗ Reduced resilience ✗ Poor problem-solving ✗ May appear overly perfect Approach: "I'm here to guide you" High demands AND high responsiveness Clear rules with explanation Democratic discussion Firm but warm Consistent consequences ✓ Responsibility and self-reliance ✓ High self-esteem ✓ Good social skills ✓ Academic achievement ✓ Secure attachment ✓ Healthy independence Establishment of Limits Provides security and structure Clear expectations reduce anxiety Safety boundaries Warmth of Support Unconditional love and acceptance Emotional safety Encouragement Neither too strict (authoritarian) nor too permissive Demands matched with support Structure with flexibility Control with understanding Explain reasons for rules Listen to child's perspective Allow input on decisions Follow through consistently Show affection regularly Provide feedback (praise and correction) Note: Research primarily Western-focused Different cultures may have different effective styles Values vary (individualism vs. collectivism) But authoritative features generally associated with positive outcomes across cultures

item.title: Perceptual Development
item.description: Research Question: When do babies understand depth perception? Mother sits on far side of "cliff" Baby placed on near side Observer watches baby's response Does baby crawl across apparent cliff? Around 6 months: Baby develops depth perception ~8 months: Mobile enough to notice/fear First crawlers: More likely to show fear (understand danger) Non-crawlers: May not show fear yet (can't move) 0-3 months: Responds to loud sounds 3-6 months: Turns to familiar voices 6-12 months: Recognizes own name 12+ months: Understands simple words 0-3 months: Responds to touch, temperature 3-6 months: Explores with mouth, hands 6-12 months: Discriminates textures (soft, rough) Cognitive development: Understand danger Motor development: Can move toward danger Memory development: Remember bad experiences Pattern recognition: Recognize threatening stimuli Provide safe exploration: Let baby explore safely Gradual challenges: Introduce novel stimuli gradually Reassurance: Be present during new experiences Don't force: Respect baby's developmental readiness Babies around 6-8 months develop fear of heights Earlier: extra dangerous (no fear restraint) Later: natural caution helps safety Still need supervision (fear not foolproof)

item.title: Personality Assessment Methods
item.description: Definition: Tests where individuals interpret ambiguous stimuli, with responses revealing their unconscious personality, conflicts, and thought processes What we project reveals our mind Unconscious shows through interpretation No "right" answer = genuine response Unique interpretations reveal personality Stimuli: 10 symmetrical inkblots Show ambiguous inkblot Ask: "What might this be?" Note: What they see, where they see it, what details they use Repeat with 10 inkblots Analyze responses Seeing "normal" things = good reality contact Seeing movement = imagination, creativity Excessive detail = obsessive thinking Ignoring color = emotional withdrawal Supporters: Reveals unconscious processes Critics: Low reliability, subjective scoring, limited predictive validity Research: Mixed results; not widely validated Stimuli: 30 ambiguous pictures (usually showing 1-3 people in unclear situation) Show ambiguous picture Ask: "Tell a story about this picture" Prompt for: What's happening? What led to it? What will happen? Record full story Analyze themes across stories Themes of failure in stories = achievement anxiety Lonely characters = isolation concerns Aggressive scenarios = anger issues Better researched than Rorschach More interpretable stories (clear content) Still subjective in scoring Used clinically but not always validated ✓ Open-ended (can't fake easily) ✓ Reveals unconscious material ✓ Rich qualitative data ✓ Good clinical interview starters ✗ Low test-retest reliability ✗ High scorer subjectivity ✗ Difficult to quantify ✗ Limited predictive validity ✗ No strong empirical support for interpretations Still used clinically Often combined with other assessments Better as exploratory than diagnostic tool More common in therapeutic settings than research

item.title: Psychoanalytic Personality Theory
item.description: Founder: Sigmund Freud and Carl JungDefinition: Inherited ideas based on ancestors' experiences that shape one's perception Inherited patterns: Biological, pre-existing Activate unconsciously: Without awareness Guide perception: What we notice, how we interpret Influence behavior: Automatic responses Show in dreams: Symbolic representations Appear in myths: Universal story patterns Integrating different archetypes Balancing light and shadow Achieving wholeness (individuation) Becoming authentic self Research Question: Can aggression be learned through observation? Participants: Young children Condition 1: Watch adult behave aggressively toward doll Condition 2: Watch adult behave calmly Control: No observation Adult either punches, kicks, or sits quietly with doll Child watches (or doesn't) Child later placed in room with similar doll Observed aggression: Children were MORE aggressive Specific actions: Imitated exact aggressive behaviors No aggression condition: Children were calm Observation: Watch behavior Encoding: Remember it Reproduction: Try the behavior Motivation: If rewarded/reinforced, repeat Personality shapes how we see environment Environment provides models and reinforcement Behavior reflects personality and changes environment All three constantly influencing each other ✓ Acknowledges unconscious processes ✓ Emphasizes early experience importance ✓ Considers defense mechanisms ✓ Widely influenced psychology ✗ Difficult to test empirically ✗ Based on clinical cases (biased sample) ✗ Overemphasizes childhood ✗ Limited scientific support ✗ Some concepts outdated Psychoanalytic ideas influential but not dominant Some concepts validated; others discarded Defense mechanisms still studied Unconscious processes confirmed by neuroscience More emphasis on biology than Freud proposed

item.title: Trait Theory
item.description: Core Principle: Personality is best understood as a set of measurable traits; everyone possesses all traits to varying degreesEveryone has: Some level of extraversion (more or less outgoing) Some level of conscientiousness (more or less organized) Some level of agreeableness (more or less sympathetic) Your unique combination creates your personalityAllport identified over 4,000 trait-related words in English! Definition: Trait so strong, person is identified with it Rarity: Very rare Example: "Machiavellian" (though not from Machiavelli himself) Effect: Dominates personality entirely Definition: Traits that best describe a person Number: Usually 5-10 main traits Example: Honest, responsible, cheerful Effect: Core to personality Definition: Traits less consistent; show situationally Context-dependent: Only appear in specific situations Example: Shy at parties but talkative with close friends Effect: Less central to personality "Rate yourself 1-7 on each trait" Person rates themselves Scored objectively Produces numerical scores Reliable and consistent Others rate the person Can compare to self-report Reveals blind spots More objective perspective ✓ Objective measurement ✓ Scientific approach ✓ Predictive validity ✓ Cross-cultural research ✓ Applied uses (job selection, compatibility) ✗ Oversimplifies personality ✗ Ignores situational factors ✗ Doesn't explain why traits exist ✗ Assumes stability (people change) ✗ Self-report bias (people not always accurate) ✗ Doesn't address motivation, values ✗ Cultural differences in trait expression Idea: Most important traits are encoded in languageProcess: Find all personality-describing words in dictionary Reduce to single traits (synonyms combined) Ask people to rate themselves Use statistics to find patterns Result: Core personality dimensions Finding: Different researchers found different numbers of core traits Two factors: Introversion-Extraversion Five factors: "Big Five" (most popular) Sixteen factors: Myers-Briggs Others: 3, 6, 7, 10 factors Match personality traits to job requirements "This job needs high conscientiousness" Compare couple's traits Identify potential conflicts Trait extremes suggest personality disorders High neuroticism → anxiety, depression Low agreeableness → antagonistic behavior Team composition Leadership potential Employee selection

item.title: Biofeedback
item.description: Definition: Process of learning to control bodily states using specialized machines that provide real-time information about physiological changesStudy: Teaching muscle relaxation through biofeedback Patients had tension headaches Measured forehead muscle tension (EMG) Provided visual feedback Taught to relax these muscles Success: Significantly reduced tension headaches Patients learned to control muscle tension Effects lasted after treatment ended See forehead tension rising → stress response Try relaxation techniques See tension drop on display → positive reinforcement Learn mind-body connection Apply skill in daily life Awareness: Real-time feedback shows the connection Control: Discover you can influence physiology Reinforcement: Success with techniques builds confidence Generalization: Learned control applies outside lab Possible Arguments:For: State of focused, narrowed attention Different brain wave patterns Relaxation response distinct from normal waking Against: Person remains fully conscious More like skill-learning than consciousness alteration Not quite the same as meditation or hypnosis Conclusion: Arguably yes—it produces sustained physiological changes distinct from normal waking consciousness

item.title: Cerebral Cortex Overview
item.description: Definition: The outer layer of the brain made of grey matter; divided into four lobes FRONTAL LOBE (Planning) | PARIETAL LOBE (Sensation) | | TEMPORAL - OCCIPITAL (Hearing) (Vision) Key Principle: Different functions are located in different parts of the brainPhineas Gage (1848): First case demonstrating localization of function Metal tamping iron pierced through frontal lobe Survived but personality changed dramatically Showed frontal lobe involved in personality/behavior Left hemisphere controls right side of body Right hemisphere controls left side of body Crossed neural pathways from brain stem Complex functions involve multiple lobes Example: Reading requires visual (occipital), language (temporal), motor (frontal) Brain can reorganize after damage Other areas can compensate for injuries More plasticity in younger brains

item.title: Dreams & Dreaming
item.description: Only dream about what we know Based on what we've seen/experienced before Can't imagine entirely novel colors or sensations Dreams remix existing memories and experiences Brain chemistry: Low norepinephrine during REM (memory hormone) Rapid fading: Dreams fade quickly upon waking No effort to encode: Dreams aren't consciously reinforced Abrupt transitions: Waking jars us from narrative Definition: Dreaming while knowing/being aware that you are dreaming Bring conscious awareness into the dream "Wake up" within the dream without waking up physically Retain some executive control Beginning to notice dream details → higher level of awareness in waking state as well Enhanced metacognition (thinking about thinking) Better recognition of patterns and inconsistencies Study: 45 undergraduates tested for creativity Boring task group: 41% more creative uses Why? Allowed mind to "incubate" the problem Moderate cognitive load (not engaging, but not idle) optimal for creativity Too much focus: Stuck in conscious constraints Too little focus: Random thought, no progress Just right: Daydreaming allows productive incubation

item.title: Frontal Lobe
item.description: Location: Front of brain (largest lobe, about 1/3 of cerebral cortex)Location: Precentral gyrus (strip running vertically near front)Function: Initiates and controls voluntary movementsLocation: Left frontal lobe (inferior frontal gyrus)Function: Speech production and language expressionNormal speech: "I went to the store and bought milk" Broca's: "I... store... buy... milk" (Function words like "to", "and", "the" are missing) Sense of self Social behavior Emotional regulation Motivation Risk assessment 1848 Railroad Accident: Metal tamping iron pierced through left frontal lobe Survived with minimal immediate neurological damage Dramatic personality changes: Responsible → irresponsible Polite → crude/profane Good-natured → irritable Cautious → reckless Significance: First clear evidence that damage to specific brain region causes specific behavioral changes Capacity: Hold 4-7 items temporarily Duration: 15-30 seconds without rehearsal Function: Essential for reasoning, problem-solving, reading comprehension Damage effect: Difficulty with complex tasks Frontal lobe has good recovery potential Other regions may compensate for motor loss Language recovery possible (especially in young people) Rehabilitation can rebuild connections

item.title: Hypnosis
item.description: Definition: Narrowed focus of attention in which people become highly suggestible to changes in behavior and thought Induction: Guide into hypnotic state Deepening: Increase depth of trance Therapeutic: Deliver suggestions Emergence: Gradually return to normal awareness Definition: Suggestion made during hypnosis that influences behavior after the session ends Suggestion planted in hypnotic state Person wakes from hypnosis Behavior/memory affected later without realizing why Controversial: Recovered memories may be false Therapist responsibility: Ethical guidelines required Not mind control: Can't make someone do something against values Definition: Reduction of pain through hypnosis Chronic pain management Surgical procedures (in some settings) Dental procedures Burn treatment Cancer pain (palliative care) Relaxation reduces muscle tension Anxiety reduction = less pain amplification Altered attention to pain signals Psychological framing changes pain interpretation Works better for some people than others Doesn't eliminate pain completely Shouldn't replace medical treatment Effect varies with susceptibility and condition

item.title: Meditation
item.description: Definition: Focusing of attention to clear one's mind and produce relaxationApproach: Mental repetition of mantra Sit with eyes closed Mentally repeat a mantra (e.g., "Om") Continue for 15-20 minutes Practice 2× per day Mantra absorbs attention Reduces random thought patterns Induces deep relaxation response Regular practice builds neurological changes Deep relaxation Reduced anxiety Improved focus Sense of inner peace Approach: Focus on present moment awareness Observe body sensations (tension, comfort) Focus on breath (natural rhythm) Notice thoughts without judgment Return attention when mind wanders Non-judgmental observation Accept what arises without trying to change it Develop awareness of mental patterns Enhanced present-moment awareness Reduced rumination Better emotional regulation Decreased anxiety Approach: Concentrate on breathing process Focus exclusively on breath Notice inhale and exhale Count breaths or use simple pattern (4-7-8) Use breath as anchor for attention Immediate calming effect Portable (can do anywhere) Provides focus point Develops concentration Activates parasympathetic nervous system Brain waves: Shift toward alpha/theta rhythms Heart rate: Decreases Blood pressure: Lowers Cortisol: Reduced (stress hormone) Parasympathetic activation: Increased Brain plasticity: Long-term meditators show structural changes

item.title: Newborn Capabilities
item.description: Key Point: Newborns have innate sensory filtering mechanisms to prevent overwhelm Trigger: Light touch on cheek Response: Head turns toward touch, mouth opens Purpose: Helps baby find breast/bottle Duration: Present at birth, fades around 3-4 months Trigger: Something placed in palm Response: Baby grips tightly Strength: Surprisingly strong for newborn Duration: Present at birth, fades around 5-6 months Trigger: Anything touches roof of mouth Response: Automatic sucking motion Purpose: Feeding Duration: Present at birth, becomes voluntary around 2-3 months Trigger: Sudden movement or loud noise Response: Arms fling out, then curl back in Purpose: Possible evolutionary protection Duration: Present at birth, fades by 5-6 months At birth: Sees light and dark, blurry Color: Can distinguish some colors Focus: Best at 8-12 inches Preference: Faces and high contrast In womb: Can hear sounds from 6-7 months gestation At birth: Responds to loud sounds Preference: Higher pitched sounds (voices) Startle: Sudden loud noises trigger Moro reflex Taste: Prefer sweet (breast milk is sweet) Smell: Recognize mother's scent Response: Turn toward familiar smells Sensitivity: More sensitive than adults to pain Temperature: Can sense temperature changes Texture: Respond to soft vs. rough surfaces Need caregiver contact and responsiveness Physical touch essential for development Emotional connection supports growth Hold close to provide security Responsive caregiving reduces stress Physical contact regulates temperature and heart rate

item.title: Parietal Lobe
item.description: Location: Top and back of brain (behind frontal, above temporal)Definition: The region of parietal lobe that receives and processes touch sensations Spatial awareness: Knowing where you are Navigation: Moving through space Object location: Judging distances Depth perception: 3D awareness Mental representation of body position Where limbs are in space Continuously updated from proprioceptors Spatial neglect: Ignoring one side of space Ataxia: Loss of coordination Constructional apraxia: Can't build/draw The parietal lobe is a sensory and spatial integration center: Receives sensory input from thalamus Processes multiple sensory types simultaneously Integrates with visual information Coordinates with motor areas for movement Touch sensations from hand (parietal) Proprioceptive feedback (parietal) Spatial location of nose (parietal) Motor command to move hand (frontal) Result: Successful coordination

item.title: The Nervous System
item.description: Function: Controls and coordinates all bodily functionsComponents: Brain: Control center for all functions Spinal Cord: Connects brain to PNS; handles reflex actions Function: Connects CNS to rest of body via branches of nerves Controls voluntary movements Transmits sensory info from skin, muscles, joints Controls involuntary functions Heart rate, digestion, hormones Activation: Threat or stress Response: Fight-or-flight Increases: Heart rate, breathing, blood pressure Decreases: Digestion, immune response Activation: Safety and calm Response: Rest-and-digest Decreases: Heart rate, breathing Increases: Digestion, immune response Action potentials travel along axon Very fast transmission All-or-nothing signal Neurotransmitters cross synaptic gap Slower than electrical Can be modulated (amplified or inhibited) Fast, automatic response Protects from immediate harm Brain learns after action taken Signal reaches brain Processing occurs Voluntary decision made Action taken Slower but more flexible

item.title: Sleep Disorders
item.description: Definition: One or more pauses in breathing or shallow breaths while sleeping Person stops breathing repeatedly during sleep Breathing resumes (usually with a gasp or snort) May wake up partially without realizing Poor sleep quality Daytime fatigue Increased risk of heart problems Can lead to sudden death if untreated Obstructive: Airways collapse during sleep Central: Brain fails to signal breathing muscles Complex: Combination of both Definition: Persistent problems falling asleep and/or staying asleep Stress and anxiety Poor sleep habits Medications Sleep environment (noise, light, temperature) Mental health conditions (depression, PTSD) Caffeine, alcohol, nicotine Daytime fatigue and irritability Difficulty concentrating Weakened immune system Increased accident risk Long-term health problems Definition: Chronic, overwhelming daytime drowsiness caused by brain's inability to regulate sleep-wake cycles normally Uncontrollable sleep attacks during day Person may fall asleep during normal activities Not simply tired — overwhelming need to sleep REM sleep enters earlier than normal May experience cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion) Brain lacks adequate hypocretin/orexin (neurotransmitter regulating wakefulness) Often caused by autoimmune condition destroying hypocretin neurons Genetic component also involved Stimulant medications (modafinil, amphetamines) Scheduled naps Lifestyle modifications Sodium oxybate (for cataplexy)

item.title: Sleep Stages
item.description: Biological clock that regulates sleep-wake cycles over approximately 24 hours Full cycle: ~90 minutes Nightly cycles: 4-5 complete cycles First REM: Short (5-10 min) Last REM: Long (30-60 min) Stage IV: Gets progressively shorter throughout night Experience hypnagogic hallucinations (hallucinations between waking and sleep) Feeling of falling Hearing your name called Sleep starts/jerks Duration: 5-10 minutes Bridge between wakefulness and sleep Light sleep Still easily awakened Some muscle twitches Duration: 20 minutes per cycle Sleep spindles: Brief bursts of rhythmic brain activity Lowered body temperature Heart rate slows Still responsive to sounds Duration: Variable Bridge between light and deep sleep Starting to enter deep sleep Harder to wake Duration: 30 minutes Deepest sleep stage Hardest to wake from Parasomnia occur here: Sleepwalking Sleep talking Night terrors Bedwetting Duration: 15-45 minutes per cycle (gets longer as night progresses) Vivid dreams and nightmares Sleep paralysis: Can't move (protective mechanism) Heart rate and breathing increase Brain wave activity resembles wakefulness Body temperature regulation fails (feel hot or cold) Enters first REM approximately 90 minutes into sleep Returns to Stage II after REM REM periods become progressively longer Most vivid, longest dreams in final REM cycles

item.title: Sensation Basics
item.description: Definition: When a stimulus activates the receptors of a sense organ; awareness of changing conditions.A stimulus is something that causes a bodily response Stimulus: Physical energy in the environment Sensation: The conscious experience in the brain Not all stimuli become sensations — many are filtered out!

item.title: Sensory Adaptation & Signal Detection
item.description: Definition: Getting used to a constant level of stimulation and only responding to changes away from that baselineDefinition: Our ability to detect stimuli depends on motivation, skill, and competing stimuli — not a fixed threshold Challenges: The traditional idea of absolute thresholds Proposes: Detection is influenced by psychological factors, not just sensory ability Airport Security Screening: High motivation to catch threats Competing stimuli (thousands of bags) Cost of miss >> cost of false alarm → Results in lower threshold (more false alarms) Happen unconsciously Very fast Don't require effort Process multiple stimuli in parallel Example: Noticing your name in a crowded room Require conscious attention Slower Require mental effort Process one thing at a time (mostly) Example: Reading a difficult textbook passage

item.title: Sensory Thresholds
item.description: Definition: The weakest amount of a stimulus required to produce a sensation Detected 50% of the time at threshold Below threshold: no sensation Above threshold: sensation guaranteed Definition: Minimum amount of difference a person can detect between two stimuli Optometrist tests: Making you choose between slightly different lenses Restaurant volume: Barely hear when someone turns up music slightly Weight lifting: Can't tell difference between 100 lb and 101 lb, but can between 100 and 110 lb "The larger or stronger a stimulus, the greater the change needed to notice any difference"K = ΔI / IWhere: K = Constant (Weber's constant) ΔI = Smallest detectable change I = Original stimulus intensity We perceive differences proportionally, not absolutely!

item.title: 02 Sleeping & Dreaming
item.description: Definition: Biological clock that regulates sleep-wake cycles Experience hallucinations (falling or hearing your name) Duration: 5-10 minutes Transition between wakefulness and sleep Duration: 20 minutes Rhythmic brain waves Lowered body temperature Heart rate slows Transition between light and deep sleep Duration: 30 minutes Sleepwalking, sleeptalking, and night terrors occur during this stage Duration: 15-45 minutes Increased eye movement, breathing, and brain activity Muscles relax Dreaming, nightmares, and sleep paralysis occur Enter REM: Approximately 90 minutes into sleep Return to Stage II Cycles: 4-5 times per night Pattern: First REM is short, but they get progressively longer Pattern: Stage 4 becomes shorter as the night progresses One or more pauses in breathing or shallow breaths while sleepingPersistent problems falling and staying asleep Chronic, overwhelming daytime drowsiness Caused by brain's inability to regulate sleep-wake cycles normally Average: 4-7 dreams per night Negative emotions are very common Only dream about what we know (based on what we've seen before) Setup: 12-minute break, then "unusual use" creativity task Groups: Resting in quiet room Difficult short-term memory task Doing something boring No break Results: Boring task group came up with 41% more creative uses Allows for creativity and problem-solving Enables mental "incubation" of problems Definition: Dreaming while knowing you are dreaming Fantasy and adventure Overcoming fears Practice skills Creativity and problem-solving Mental health Bonus: Beginning to notice details → higher level of awareness in awake state as well

item.title: 03 Altered States of Consciousness
item.description: Definition: Any condition which differs from a normal waking state Note: Induced changes are almost always temporaryProcess of learning to control bodily states using specialized machines Machines tell a person about subtle bodily changes including: Brain waves Heart rate Skin temperature Sweat-gland activity Person tries different thoughts and feelings while watching their effect on the body Thomas Budzyński (1973): Taught patients to relax muscles in the forehead to reduce tension headaches Treating PTSD ADHD Depression Anxiety Why is biofeedback considered an altered state of consciousness?Focusing of attention to clear one's mind and produce relaxation Lower blood pressure Lower heart rate Lower respiratory rate Help with stress, insomnia, etc. Mental repetition of a mantra (e.g., Om) Practice: Sit with eyes closed and meditate for 15-20 minutes 2× a day Focus on the present moment Attention on: body, breath, and thoughts Concentrate on breathing process Provides focus and sense of calm Narrowed focus of attention; people become highly suggestible to changes in behavior and thought Shifting Perceptions — Alter how reality is perceived Focus — On one small aspect of reality Relaxation — Forget outside anxiety Trust — Increase cooperation with suggestions Suggestion made during hypnosis that influences behavior after the session Helps to recall or suppress certain information Reduction of pain Mechanism: Helps patient relax and reduce anxiety → lessens perception of pain Clinical use: Habits and phobias

item.title: 04 Brain & Nervous System
item.description: Function: Controls the bodyNervous System ├── Central Nervous System (CNS) │ ├── Brain │ └── Brain Stem └── Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) └── Branches of nerves off to the sides Electrical signals: Throughout the neuron Chemical signals: Neurotransmitters across the synapse Definition: Chemicals produced in the cell Stress Diet Toxins Genetics Drugs Alcohol Caffeine Acetylcholine → Alzheimer's disease Dopamine → Schizophrenia Dopamine → Parkinson's disease Serotonin → Depression Heartbeat Digestion Mood Sleep Concentration Weight After release, neurotransmitters have two options: Transmission: Information is passed to new cell Inhibition: Signal stops Definition: The outer layer of the brain made of grey matter Structure: Divided into four lobes Hearing Some speech Memory Function: Language comprehension Damage result: Wernicke's Aphasia Can speak well Cannot understand what is being said Produces "word salad" Sensory information (touch, temperature, pressure, etc.) Visuospatial processing (your position in space) The larger area of the brain a body part takes up, the more sensitive the area is Creates a distorted "sensory map" Planning Reasoning Movement (motor ability) Personality Working memory Creative thinking and problem-solving Key principle: The larger area of the brain a body part takes up, the more complex the movements are Creates a distorted motor "map" with disproportionate space for hands, lips, tongue Function: Language production Damage result: Can understand speech but cannot form words Visual processing Processes: color, form, motion, location Significance: First case showing different functions are located in different parts of the brainDetails: Metal tamping iron went through his frontal lobe; resulted in personality and behavioral changes

item.title: 05 Human Development
item.description: Complete protection from sensory overload Grasping reflex Rooting reflex Capabilities for basic survival Definition: Maturation — internally programmed growth of a child; plays a key role in progress of motor skills Around 6 months, babies start to understand depth perception Demonstrated through visual cliff apparatus (apparent drop-off) Between 2 and 5 years: typical child learns an average of 10 words per day (nearly 1 word every hour awake) Imitation → 2. Overgeneralization → 3. Rule-governed language Nature vs. Nurture: Which plays a larger role? Critical Period: Sensitive period early in life in which language acquisition is easier "Bosses" No need to explain actions or demands Child has no right to question Kids have final say No rules/demands No expectations Parents give up their parenting role Self-centered Uncommitted to being a parent Distant from child Hover over their children Want to know and have a say in every aspect of child's life Pay very close attention Kids participate in decisions Parents have right to veto Discussions occur Key Factors: Establishment of limits (structure) Warmth of support (love) Developmental Gains: Development of responsibility Parents viewed as sources of love and respect Development of cooperative independence

item.title: 06 Personality Theories
item.description: Tests where individuals interpret ambiguous stimuli, revealing their personality Interpretation of inkblot images Reveals unconscious processes and personality patterns Individuals create stories about ambiguous images Reveals themes, concerns, and motivations Personal Unconscious: Individual repressed thoughts and experiences Collective Unconscious: Inherited instincts, urges, and memories of all humans Definition: Inherited ideas based on ancestors' experiences Function: Shape one's perception of the world Examples: The Hero, The Shadow, The Wise Old Man Looked for personality of an aggressive person Demonstrated that aggression can be learned through observation and modeling Ideas of oneself, of others, and of the world shape personalities Definition: Mental representation of people, events, and concepts Function: Determine how we perceive things and respond to them Strive for self-actualization (one's unique potential) Developed concept of self-actualization Believed in human potential and growth Focused on "The Self" Emphasized unconditional positive regard Realistically oriented Accept the world as it is Spontaneous Creative Resist conformity Independent Definition: View of yourself based on positive interactions Conditions of worth: Conditions one must meet to feel positivity about oneself Unconditional positive regard: Perception that significant others value you in your entirety Everyone possesses all traits Traits can be quantified The amount of each trait determines your personality Most well-known trait theory — central for all peopleBased on Carl Jung's writingsJung presented 4 ways in which people experience the world: 16 types total (2^4 combinations) Preferences: Not better or worse; just different styles Examples: INTJ, ENFP, ISTJ, ENFJ, etc.
